text.p: Siemens India Ltd, reeling under an 845-million-rupee loss in its 1996/97 (April-March) results, said on Friday it had ridden out one of the most difficult years in its history, but hoped to bounce back within 12 months.
"This fiscal year for Siemens has been one of the most difficult ones faced in our 75-year history," Siemens managing director Juergen Schubert told a news conference.
The loss proved to be nearly double that of analysts' earlier projections of 450 million rupees, compared to a net profit of 372 million rupees in 1995/96.
The firm said in a statement its new orders had declined 18 percent to 11.85 billion rupees, against 14.46 billion in the previous 12-month period.
Schubert traced Siemens' troubles to the slowdown in India's industrial growth in the first half of 1996/97.
He said this was further aggravated by the inadequate supply of credit to industry coupled with high interest rates which in turn resulted in a drop in public and private investments.
"This dramatic change from extreme growth to stagnation of the market within such a short timeframe surprised industry generally and surprised Siemens also in its intensity," he said.
But Schubert was optimistic Siemens would recover quickly.

"With the market situation as it is, and environmental changes we are faced with, we have to align our operations to ensure that the company bounces back to profitability in the next 12-18 months," he said.
Siemens' turnover rose 10 percent, to 11.67 billion, in the 12-months to March 31, as compared to 10.58 billion in the previous 12-month period, the statement said.
Siemens' move from electro-mechanical products to electronic products had seen a tremendous drop in the actual added value in its factories, Schubert said.
Siemens had attempted to compensate for this with fast growth in previous years, but was now forced to switch tracks.
"Due to the abrupt and negative repercussions of the economic environment, we must now revise this strategy," Schubert said.
"We have to reduce earlier planned production volumes and also need to adjust all our resources to the reduced volumes."
Customers' ability to pay had also been badly affected, with overdue payments increasing considerably, Schubert said.
"We stop supplies if payments cannot be expected with some confidence," he added. "But initially this results in higher inventories and lower turnover."
The firm also had to defer some of its planned investments as a result of the poor economic scenario, Schubert said.

In a statement, Siemens attributed the loss to its discontinuation of telecommunications operations, to be hived off to a new firm, Siemens Public Communications Networks Ltd as well as to the cost of restructuring its business operations.
In addition, the operations of its main business had deteriorated due to higher operational costs, lower capacity utilisation, higher interest and risk burden, Siemens said.
Earlier analysts had forecast that slow growth in power, telecommunications and capital goods would result in a net loss of about 450 million rupees.
"We're not too late reacting," executive director Heinz-Joachim Neubuerger said, replying to a question why Siemens had not anticipated the fall-out of the slowdown.

"The management together with the employees is building up momentum and broadbased support in the company to do what we have to do to benchmark international standards, unlike other companies that may face these issues but are not debating them yet," Neubuerger added.
Siemens India is a unit of Germany's Siemens AG,
